value: 5! = 120 seatings (the chairs are of DIFFERENT COLOURS, so they are distinguishable seats and rotations are NOT equivalent). If the chairs were identical the answer would be 4! = 24.
why: The clause 'five chairs of different colours' is precisely what makes each seat distinguishable, so a rotation moves every boy to a different-coloured chair and produces a genuinely new arrangement: the count is 5! = 120, which is absent from the options. Option A (24) is the answer to the version WITHOUT the colour clause, i.e. the ordinary circular permutation (n-1)! = 4!; the stem's own distinguishing clause contradicts it.

value: Maximum number of triangles = C(m+n+k,3) - C(m,3) - C(n,3) - C(k,3)
why: Choose any 3 of the m+n+k points and discard the triples that are collinear, i.e. those lying wholly on L1, L2 or L3 - that removes THREE terms, one per line. Option B drops the -C(k,3) term entirely; verified by exhaustive enumeration over generic point positions (m,n,k = 3,3,3 gives max 81, while A=84, B=82, C=86; 4,3,5 gives 205 vs A=220, B=215, C=225), so none of A/B/C matches and 'None of these' is correct.
1+x+x^2+x^3 = (1+x)(1+x^2), so the expression is (1+x)^10 (1+x^2)^10 and the x^2 coefficient is C(10,2)*1 + 1*C(10,1) = 45 + 10 = 55; confirmed by full sympy expansion of (1+x+x^2+x^3)^10.

value: No real x exists: with t = 5^x the A.P. condition gives (t-1)^2 = 2(t - 11/5), i.e. t^2 - 4t + 27/5 = 0, whose discriminant is -28/5 < 0.
why: 2*log_3(5^x - 1) = log_3 2 + log_3(5^x - 11/5) reduces to 5t^2 - 20t + 27 = 0 (discriminant 400 - 540 = -140), so the printed stem has no solution at all and every option is wrong; each offered t value (2, 3, 5, 6) was also tested numerically at 40 dps and none gives equal successive differences. The stem is almost certainly corrupt: with the first term log_3 6 instead of log_3 2 and the third log_3(5^x - 11/6) instead of 11/5, the equation becomes t^2 - 8t + 12 = 0 with both roots admissible, giving exactly option D (log_5 6 and log_5 2); log_3 6 with 7/3 in place of 11/5 would instead give option B (1 and log_5 3).

P^2 = P(QP) = (PQ)P = QP = P and Q^2 = Q(PQ) = (QP)Q = PQ = Q, so P^2 + Q^2 = P + Q. Verified on a concrete non-trivial pair P = [[1,1],[0,0]], Q = [[1,0],[0,0]] with P != Q, which satisfies both hypotheses and rules out A, B and D.

d is the constant term, i.e. the determinant evaluated at u = 0: |0,1,-1; -3,0,2; 3,-4,0| = 0 - 1(0-6) + (-1)(12-0) = 6 - 12 = -6; sympy's full cubic expansion confirms the constant coefficient is -6.
The matrix is I + v v^T with v = (a,b,c)^T, so its determinant is 1 + v^T v = 1 + a^2 + b^2 + c^2; sympy expansion gives exactly a^2+b^2+c^2+1 and symbolically disproves the other three options.

C1 -> C1 - C2 makes column 1 equal (2a, 2a, 0)^T; pulling out 2a and doing R2 -> R2 - R1 leaves 2a * [(2b+c)*3 - 3c] = 2a * 6b = 12ab. Checked at the discriminating point a=2, b=5, c=7 where det = 120 = 12ab, separating it from -12ab = -120 and ab = 10.

Writing X = ln x, Y = ln y, Z = ln z, the three rows are (1/Z)(X,Y,Z), (1/X)(X,Y,Z) and (1/Y)(X,Y,Z) - all scalar multiples of the same vector - so the rows are linearly dependent and the determinant vanishes identically. Confirmed symbolically and numerically at 50 dps for (x,y,z) = (2,3,5), (7,11,13) and (1.7,4.3,9.1), each giving exactly 0.

value: det(adj P) = 64. Explicitly adj P = 4*I3 and det(4*I3) = 4^3 = 64 = (det P)^(n-1) = 8^2.
why: det(adj P) is the SCALAR 64 = 2^6, and option C is the only option numerically consistent with it once 'P^6' is read as 2^6. Strictly the options are ill-typed: P^6 as a matrix is 64*I3, not the scalar 64, and if the options were meant as |P|^k then |P|^6 = 8^6 = 262144, so a literal reading would force D. Low confidence is a notation defect in the options, not a doubt about the value.

det is multiplicative, so det(B^-1 A B) = det(B^-1) det(A) det(B) = (1/det B) det(A) det(B) = det(A); similar matrices always share a determinant. B is non-singular so det(B) != 0 and the cancellation is legitimate.

With p = 1/6 per throw and A throwing first, P(A) = p(1 + q^2 + q^4 + ...) = p/(1-q^2) = (1/6)/(11/36) = 6/11 and P(B) = qp/(1-q^2) = 5/11, summing to 1; exact Fraction arithmetic plus a 4000-term truncated series both give 6/11. The starter must have the LARGER share, which fixes the order and rules out the swapped option B.

The number is odd exactly when the units digit is 1 or 3, i.e. 2 of the 4 equally likely last digits, so P = 2*3!/4! = 12/24 = 1/2. Confirmed by enumerating all 24 permutations of 1234 (12 are odd). 1/2 is not among 'zero', 1/3 or 1/4, so 'None of these' is correct.

A non-leap year is 52 weeks plus exactly ONE odd day, so precisely one weekday occurs 53 times and it is equally likely to be any of the 7; 'Friday or Saturday' covers 2 of those 7 mutually exclusive cases, giving 2/7. Enumerating all 7 possible starting weekdays gives 2 favourable. Option A (3/7) is the LEAP-year answer (two odd days, 3 favourable pairs) and is the distractor here.

Bayes: P(unbiased | H) = (1/2 * 1/2) / (1/2 * 1/2 + 1/2 * 3/4) = (1/4)/(5/8) = 2/5; exact Fraction arithmetic confirms. Option A (2/3) would be the answer if the biased coin had probability 1/4 of heads, and C (1/2) is the prior, not the posterior.
